# Psychotherapy and defense mechanisms

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Psychiatry > Psychology, ethics, and counseling > Psychotherapy and defense mechanisms*

[Original Article Link](/library/PN0WYg)

---

## Summary

<u>Psychotherapy</u> is the use of psychological methods to help patients modify undesirable emotions, attitudes, and behaviors. The most common types of <u>psychotherapy</u> are <u>psychoanalysis</u>, <u>behavioral therapy</u>, <u>cognitive therapy</u>, <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u>, <u>dialectical behavioral therapy</u>, <u>motivational interviewing</u>, <u>group therapy</u>, <u>couples therapy</u>, <u>family therapy</u>, and <u>schema therapy</u>. <u>Psychoanalytic theory</u> has its origin in Freud's topographic and <u>structural theories</u>. According to Freud, <u>defense mechanisms</u> help individuals to mediate their reactions to internal emotional conflicts triggered by external stressors. <u>Defense mechanisms</u> are categorized into four levels: pathological, immature, neurotic, and <u>mature defenses</u>. This article examines <u>mature defense</u> mechanisms, which manifest in healthy adults, as well as pathological, neurotic, and <u>immature defense</u> mechanisms, all of which are associated with psychiatric disorders.

## Psychoanalysis

* Description

* Focuses on improving awareness of repressed feelings and experiences

* Aims to resolve conflicts in the subconscious (e.g., by studying dreams)

* A strong therapeutic alliance (i.e., the bond between therapist and patient) is important for successful <u>psychoanalysis</u> therapy.

* Countertransference: a complication in which the therapist projects unconscious feelings onto the patient (e.g., the therapist sees the patient as a sibling)

* Indications

* <u>Personality disorders</u> (<u>clusters</u> B and <u>cluster C</u>)

* <u>Anxiety disorders</u>

* Sexual disorders (e.g., <u>sexual dysfunction</u>, <u>paraphilic disorders</u>) [[3]](/library/4Eb3Dv)[[4]](/library/kEbmDv)

* <u>Depressive disorders</u>

* Healthy individuals under <u>stress</u>

* <u>Somatic symptom disorders</u>

* Duration: 3–5 times per week for years

* Techniques

* Transference

* The patient projects unconscious feelings about significant persons in their childhood onto the therapist (e.g., the therapist is treated as a parental figure).

* The therapist can gain insight into personal conflicts by interpreting these feelings.

* Free association: The patient describes all thoughts that spontaneously occur during the therapy session.

* Dream interpretation: identifying representations of the patient's urges and fears in their dreams to gain insight into subconscious conflicts

---

## Psychodynamic psychotherapy

* Description

* Similar to <u>psychoanalysis</u> but with less of an emphasis on dream analysis

* Focuses on developing insight into and changing current behaviors, feelings, and thoughts by analyzing past experiences

* Aims to gain insight into unconscious mental processes

* The therapist aims to remain as neutral as possible, to allow the patient to develop their own interpretations.

* Indications

* <u>Anxiety disorders</u>

* <u>Depressive disorders</u>

* <u>Personality disorders</u>

* <u>Anorexia nervosa</u>

* Duration: once weekly for 6 months to years

* Techniques

* Patient education: informing the patient about their condition and about the principles of <u>psychodynamic therapy</u>

* The therapist takes a very thorough history to identify stressors and core patterns in the patient's behavior.

* Promoting a strong <u>therapeutic alliance</u>

---

## Supportive psychotherapy

* Description

* Focuses on identifying maladaptive behavioral patterns and problematic interpersonal relationships

* Aims to help the patient maintain hope and cope with life challenges

* Aims to improve the patient's self-esteem, adaptive skills, and behavioral functioning (i.e., performance in social environments)

* Indications

* <u>Anxiety disorders</u>

* <u>Depressive disorders</u>

* Coping with a crisis or a transient problem

* Duration

* Open-ended, from days to years

* The weekly frequency is flexible and determined by the severity of symptoms and the patient's progress.

* Techniques

* Promotion of a strong <u>therapeutic alliance</u> by following a <u>patient-centered approach</u> (i.e., expressing interest, empathy, and acceptance)

* The therapist provides reinforcement, encouragement, and guidance on available resources.

* <u>Patient counseling</u> (often used as an adjunctive treatment)

---

## Interpersonal therapy

* Description

* Focuses on identifying and analyzing problematic interpersonal relationships (e.g., <u>unresolved grief</u> or conflicts) and/or life situations (e.g., change in jobs, geographical move)

* Aims to improve communication skills and control over mood and behavior

* Indications

* <u>Depressive disorders</u>

* <u>Eating disorders</u>

* Duration: weekly sessions for 12–16 weeks

* Techniques

* Medical model: The disease the patient suffers from (e.g., <u>depressive disorder</u>) is a clinical syndrome distinct from the patient's <u>personality</u> and should be explained similarly to other medical conditions (e.g., <u>diabetes</u>).

* Identifying connections between the disease manifestation and life events (e.g., the connection between the <u>death</u> of a loved one and the development of an <u>eating disorder</u>)

---

## Behavioral therapy

* Description

* Focuses on helping the patient to identify, reflect, and change maladaptive behavior that is triggered by specific stimuli (e.g., fear of spiders)

* Aims to teach the patient possible alternatives to maladaptive behavior

* Usually combined with <u>cognitive therapy</u> as <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u>

* Indications

* <u>Phobias</u>

* <u>Bipolar disorder</u>

* <u>Borderline personality disorder</u> (<u>BPD</u>)

* <u>Obsessive compulsive disorder</u> (<u>OCD</u>)

* <u>Panic disorders</u>

* <u>PTSD</u>

* <u>Psychosis</u>

* Duration: brief (5–20 sessions) [[7]](/library/B-Xzz00)

* Techniques

* <u>Conditioning</u>

* <u>Classical conditioning</u>

* <u>Operant conditioning</u>

* <u>Extinction (psychology)</u>

* <u>Deconditioning</u>

* <u>Systemic desensitization</u>

* <u>Flooding</u>

* <u>Implosion</u>

* <u>Biofeedback</u>

* <u>Token economy</u>

* <u>Aversion therapy</u>

---

## Cognitive therapy

* Description

* Focuses on identifying and correcting faulty assumptions;   and negative thoughts

* Aims to improve patient awareness of emotions and thoughts

* Usually combined with <u>behavioral therapy</u> as <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u>

* Indications

* <u>Major depressive disorder</u>

* <u>Paranoid personality disorder</u>

* <u>Somatic symptom disorders</u>

* <u>Anxiety disorders</u>

* <u>OCD</u>

* <u>Eating disorders</u>

* Duration: brief (5–10 sessions)

* Techniques: relies mainly on thought exercises

* Guided questioning: directing the patient's behavior and <u>thought process</u> toward a therapeutic goal by asking a series of graded questions

* Journaling (psychiatry): The patient writes down their thoughts, feelings, and internal experiences to better understand their own ideas and emotions.

* Self-monitoring by journaling behaviors, thoughts, and feelings (e.g., treatment for an <u>eating disorder</u> includes monitoring food intake by writing down every meal and the emotions/thoughts attached to eating)

* Enables identification of triggers and problematic chains of behavior (e.g., <u>stress</u>-induced binge eating)

* Cognitive restructuring: The patient identifies negative automatic thoughts (i.e., dysfunctional/negative view of the self, future, or world) in order to dispute them and eventually replace them with healthy <u>thought processes</u>.

---

## Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)

* Description

* Focuses on changing distorted, harmful, irrational, or ineffective beliefs, attitudes, and behavior patterns that lead to dysfunctional behaviors

* Helps the patient to identify unhelpful and distorted thoughts

* Helps the patient develop skills and strategies to alter abnormal behaviors and develop healthy <u>coping mechanisms</u>

* Aims to improve the patient's control over their emotions and ability to deal with <u>distress</u>

* Indications

* <u>OCD</u>

* <u>Trauma-related disorders</u>

* <u>Schizophrenia</u>

* <u>Substance use disorders</u>

* <u>Phobias</u>

* <u>Depressive disorders</u>

* <u>Anxiety disorders</u>

* <u>Eating disorders</u>

* Duration

* Usually for approx. 16 weeks

* Twice weekly for the first 4 weeks

* Once weekly for the remaining 12 weeks

* Techniques: combines techniques from <u>cognitive therapy</u> and <u>behavioral therapy</u>

* <u>Cognitive restructuring</u>

* <u>Journaling (psychiatry)</u>

* <u>Systemic desensitization</u>

* Patient education

* The patient is encouraged to implement new skills;  (e.g., discussing a faulty assumption with friends) or to set behavioral tasks (e.g., a patient with an <u>eating disorder</u> is asked to eat a feared food like ice cream) outside of therapeutic sessions.

* Subtypes and variants: exposure and response prevention [[9]](/library/qCXCGZ0)

* A type of <u>CBT</u> in which the patient is guided through repeated and prolonged exposures to situations that provoke <u>anxiety</u> and/or obsessive thoughts and is encouraged to avoid <u>compulsive behaviors</u>

* Indication: <u>OCD</u>

---

## Dialectical behavioral therapy

* Description

* Focuses on teaching new skills (e.g., relaxation techniques)

* Aims to reduce unhealthy and self-destructive behavior

* Indications

* <u>BPD</u>

* <u>Depressive disorder</u> associated with <u>suicidal thoughts</u>

* <u>Chronic pain</u>

* <u>Eating disorders</u>

* <u>Trauma-related disorders</u>

* Duration: once weekly for approx. 16 weeks

* Techniques

* Mindfulness: a complex field that revolves around being fully present and aware of one's thoughts, feelings, and actions (e.g., practicing guided breathing, yoga asanas, <u>meditation</u>)

* Emotional regulation: The patient is taught to become aware of their emotions and to assess them rationally.

* Distress tolerance: The patient learns to better handle crises and stressful situations.

* Interpersonal effectiveness: The patient is trained to recognize and assert their needs without coming into conflict with others.





> [!NOTE]
> MEDI: Mindfulness, Emotional regulation, Distress tolerance, and Interpersonal <u>effectiveness</u> are techniques of <u>dialectical behavioral therapy</u>

---

## Motivational interviewing

### Overview




* Description

* A <u>patient-centered</u> counseling approach designed to promote behavioral change

* Empowers patients to explore and resolve ambivalence toward change, identify goals for change, generate motivation to change, and reinforce a commitment to change

* Indications

* <u>Substance use disorders</u>

* <u>Depressive disorders</u>

* Conditions requiring lifestyle changes (e.g., <u>obesity</u>, smoking)

* Poor treatment and <u>medication adherence</u>

* DEARS principles

* Determine discrepancy: Collaborate with the patient on determining what stands in the way of their will to change.

* Express empathy: Develop an understanding of the patient's perspective and reflect that understanding back to them.

* Avoid arguments: Avoid imposing your perspective of the issues standing in the way of change and their resolution on the patient.

* Roll with Resistance: Accept that the patient may resist change.

* Support <u>self-efficacy</u>: Help the patient develop their belief in and their capacity to adopt behaviors that effectuate change.

* OARS skills and techniques

* Open-ended questions: Invite patients to relate their experiences and perspectives rather than guide them in a certain direction with <u>leading questions</u>.

* Affirmation: Recognize the patient's strengths and acknowledge behaviors associated with positive change.

* Reflective listening: Listen closely to and reflect on what the patient is saying and ensure you understand their perspectives and experiences.

* Summaries: Recap the main points of a conversation at regular intervals, esp. at points of transition.





### Processes



1. * Engaging: establishing a working relationship based on trust

* Provide an environment that makes the patient feel comfortable and safe.

* Focus on building rapport with the patient, affirming their strengths, encouraging their <u>autonomy</u>, and addressing their questions.

* Make an effort to understand and develop empathy for the patient's perspective using <u>reflective listening</u>.
2. * Focusing: working with the patient to identify the desired change and develop an agenda to achieve it

* Support the patient in defining a specific, clear, and relevant goal.

* Set an agenda to achieve the change collaboratively.

* Understand the reasons and values behind the goal for change.
3. * Evoking: bringing forth the patient's own motivations and thoughts for change

* Listen carefully for language related to change.

* Support and encourage the patient's ideas and motivations reflected by language related to change.

* Collaborate with the patient to understand the emotions associated with change.

* Avoid challenging the patient if they are resistant to change or use language that moves them away from change.

* Ask questions to guide the patient toward change.

* Support the patient in developing and nurturing their intrinsic motivation.
4. * Planning: support the patient in developing a plan of action based on their own insight and experiences to reinforce their commitment to change.

* Summarize the content of previous interviews and reiterate past successes.

* Collaborate on defining actions that bring about change and how to measure the success of these actions.

* Support the patient in identifying and removing any barriers to change.

---

## Group therapy

* Description

* Aims to form a support network for individuals with similar diseases or difficulties

* Allows direct interaction between therapists and patients, and direct interaction between patients

* Certain groups can be peer-lead and do not need to have a therapist present (e.g., <u>Alcoholics Anonymous</u>).

* Indications

* <u>Personality disorders</u>

* <u>Substance use disorders</u>

* Family and group disorders

* <u>Bereavement</u>

* Chronic or life-threatening conditions (e.g., <u>diabetes</u>, cancer)

* Duration: once weekly for months to years

* Techniques: one or more therapists help the group to solve emotional difficulties using various techniques

* <u>Psychoeducation</u>

* Cognitive techniques (e.g., <u>cognitive restructuring</u>)

* Supportive techniques (e.g., <u>patient counseling</u>, providing resources, guidance, and encouragement)

---

## Family therapy

* Description

* Focuses on identifying and resolving familial dysfunctions and problems of individual members that affect the family as a whole

* Aims to improve communication skills between family members

* Aims to reduce and/or solve conflict

* Emphasizes family strengths to overcome identified dysfunctions

* Promotes a supportive environment

* Indications

* Behavioral problems in family members (e.g., antisocial behavior in <u>adolescents</u>, substance use)

* Conflict between parents, siblings, or parents and children

* Changes and other challenges within the family (e.g., illness, divorce, <u>death</u>, relocation)

* Trauma

* Psychiatric disorders in family members (e.g., ; <u>major depressive disorder</u>, <u>bipolar disorder</u>, <u>substance use disorders</u>, <u>schizophrenia</u>;  )

* Techniques

* <u>Psychoeducation</u>

* Education of family members about a psychiatric disorder that affects a family member

* Introduction of techniques that family members can use to cope with the circumstances

* <u>Cognitive behavioral therapy</u>

---

## Couples therapy

* Description: aims to reduce conflicts and improve communication skills between couples

* Indications

* Sexual disorders

* Motivated couples who are not suffering severe mental illness

* Duration: once weekly for weeks to years

* Techniques

* Conjoint therapy: One therapist sees the couple together.

* Concurrent therapy: Each person is seen separately by the same therapist.

* Collaborative therapy: Each person is seen by a separate therapist.

* Four-way therapy: Two therapists see the couple together (especially for sexual disorders).

---

## Psychoanalytic theory

### Topographic Freudian model [[22]](/library/mgYVDo)




* Conscious (psychiatry)

* Current awareness of ongoing thoughts and experiences

* Secondary process thinking (e.g., logic, reasoning)

* Preconscious (psychiatry)

* A level below conscious awareness

* Repressed memories and/or thoughts of which one is not presently aware but are easily called into conscious awareness

* Unconscious (psychiatry)

* Primitive primary process thinking (e.g., sex, aggression)

* Normally repressed from conscious awareness because of negative associations (e.g., feelings of shame or guilt)

* Plays a more prominent role in the behavior of adult individuals with mental illness (e.g., <u>psychosis</u>) and in children





### Structural Freudian model [[23]](/library/l9bvnD)[[24]](/library/N9b-nD)




* Id (psychiatry): unconscious; source of drive and instinctive impulses (e.g., sex, aggression, illogical)

* Super-ego (psychiatry)

* Represents both the consciousness and the idealized self

* Responsible for rational and reality-oriented thought

* Ego (psychiatry)

* Mediates between environment, id, and super-ego

* Employs <u>defense mechanisms</u>





### Carl Jung theory [[25]](/library/oDb02D)




* <u>Ego (psychiatry)</u>

* Conscious mind

* Current awareness of emotions, thoughts, and memories

* Personal unconscious (psychiatry)

* Similar to the Freudian unconscious

* Repressed memories and complexes (an organization of an individual's thoughts, feelings, attitudes, and memories concerning a particular concept)

* Collective unconscious (psychiatry)

* Shared with other humans

* Based on latent memories from the ancestral and evolutionary past, which shape the characteristics of the human species





#### Jungian archetypes




Some of the most important archetypes Carl Jung proposed include:




* Persona (psychiatry): the public presentation of the self; the real self is concealed to adapt to social norms or expectations

* Anima/animus (psychiatry): the unconscious, countersexual aspect of the biological sex in the human psyche

* Shadow (psychiatry): repressed and unconscious; source of instinctive, irrational impulses

* Self (psychiatry): overarching structure of the individual; unification of male and female and of unconscious and conscious





### Theory of schema therapy




* <u>Schema therapy</u> was developed by Jeffrey Young.

* It is based on the notion that people acquire certain basic schemas (i.e., mental structures) that help them interpret and organize information and thereby establish certain behavioral patterns throughout the course of their lives.

* These schemas, in part, set the conditions for meeting psychological needs and therefore also influence behavior.

* E.g., childhood trauma can lead to maladaptive schemas that are difficult to access consciously and may be the root cause of a <u>personality disorder</u>.





### <u>Stages of psychosocial development according to Erik Erikson</u> [[26]](/library/wKchiW0)[[27]](/library/epcxoW0)




* Eight sequential <u>stages of psychosocial development</u> that determine the psychological characteristics and core beliefs an individual develops during their lifetime

* Each stage is characterized by an opposing tendency with which an individual is confronted and must resolve in order to develop a positive, adaptive or negative, maladaptive trait

* Psychosocial development is considered a lifelong process of continuously reevaluating and reintegrating the eight stages.





| Stages of psychosocial development according to Erik Erikson |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stage | Period | Opposing tendencies | Adaptive trait | Factors that promote the development of adaptive traits |
| Stage 1 | <u>Infancy</u> | Basic trust vs. basic mistrust | Hope | Fulfillment of emotional and physical needs (e.g., experiencing reliability and affection, access to food) |
| Stage 2 | Early childhood | <br><u>Autonomy</u> vs. shame, doubt | Will | Establishing a balance between dependence/safety and independence/self-control<br> |
| Stage 3 | Play age | Initiative vs. guilt | Purpose | Encouragement and guidance in social interactions, self-assertion, and cooperation |
| Stage 4 | School age | Industry vs. inferiority <br> | Competence | Reasonable academic expectations, reinforcing initiative, providing praise for accomplishments |
| Stage 5 | <u>Adolescence</u> | Identity integration vs. identity confusion | Fidelity | Exploration of <u>self-identity</u>, personal goals, sexual and occupational experiences |
| Stage 6 | Young adulthood | Intimacy vs. isolation | Love | Formation of friendships and relationships |
| Stage 7 | Adulthood | Generativity vs. stagnation, self-absorption <br> | Care | Involvement in community, contributing to society, engaging with younger generations (e.g., parenting, teaching) |
| Stage 8 | Old age | Integrity vs. despair | Wisdom | <br><u>Retrospection</u> and recognition of life accomplishments |

## Defense mechanisms

### Overview [[28]](/library/RgYlEo)




* Definition

* Primary tools of the ego used to cope with external stressors to avoid or reduce <u>anxiety</u>, restrict impulses, and avoid unpleasant feelings

* Mostly unconscious

* Classification

* Level 1 – Pathological/narcissistic: seen in children and in adult individuals with <u>personality disorders</u>

* Level 2 – Immature (primitive): common in patients with <u>personality disorders</u>, patients suffering from <u>psychosis</u>, individuals with <u>anxiety disorders</u>, children, and <u>adolescents</u>

* Level 3 – Neurotic: common in patients with <u>OCD</u> and/or <u>anxiety</u>

* Level 4 – Mature (sophisticated): seen in normal adults





### Pathological defenses [[29]](/library/Uvbbzv)[[30]](/library/KDbU2D)




| Overview of pathological defenses |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Description | Examples |
| Splitting (psychiatry) | <br><br>* An all or nothing view about a subject or person<br><br>* Affected individuals are unable to integrate positive and negative images into a cohesive whole.<br><br>* Can affect both the sense of self and others<br><br>* Can manifest in extreme prejudice/stereotyping<br><br>* Associated with <u>BPD</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* A boy dislikes his mother's best friend, who is a teacher, just because he despises all teachers.<br><br>* A woman is convinced that all student counselors are good people based on their choice of profession alone.<br><br><br> |
| Projection (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Attributing one's undesired feelings or thoughts to another person<br><br>* In patients with <u>paranoid personality disorder</u>, may include <u>paranoid</u> <u>delusions</u>, and acting on these perceptions<br><br>* Projection is a form of externalization.<br><br>* Distinct from displacement<br><br>* Projection: The affected individual extends emotions/thoughts about themselves to another person.<br><br>* Displacement: The affected individual shifts emotions/thoughts about one person to a less threatening person or object.<br><br>* Projective identification: When the individual onto whom emotions/thoughts are being projected internalizes these qualities and believes them to be true.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* A clinician believes that a patient dislikes him when in reality he dislikes the patient.<br><br>* A man fears that his wife is cheating on him while he himself feels attracted to other women.<br><br><br> |
| Denial (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Avoiding <u>anxiety</u>-provoking thoughts by not accepting reality<br><br>* Common early response to bad news<br><br>* Associated with <u>substance use disorder</u><br><br><br> | <br>* An elderly woman refuses to acknowledge a cancer diagnosis by planning a vacation despite imminent <u>chemotherapy</u> appointments.<br><br> |
| Distortion (psychiatry) | <br>* Altered perception of external reality (e.g., <u>hallucinations</u>, wish-fulfilling <u>delusions</u>) to suit inner needs to sustain superiority/entitlement<br><br> | <br>* A woman tells a story about how she was abandoned by her family when she actually ran away from home.<br><br> |





### Immature defenses [[31]](/library/qGbCZv)




| Overview of immature defenses |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Description | Examples |
| Acting out (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Expressing unacceptable or extreme feelings and thoughts through action<br><br>* Associated with borderline and antisocial <u>personality disorders</u><br><br><br> | <br>* An employee yells and throws things from his desk in response to the news of being fired from his job.<br><br> |
| Regression (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Involuntary return to a childlike state or prior maturational stage to avoid the <u>stress</u> evoked at the present level of development<br><br>* Associated with <u>dependent personality disorder</u><br><br>* Common in individuals who are feeling ill, tired, or uncomfortable (compare with fixation)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* A previously toilet-trained child begins to wet the bed again after the <u>birth</u> of a new sibling.<br><br>* A child who stopped sucking their thumb begins to do so again after being hospitalized for an upcoming <u>surgery</u>.<br><br><br> |
| Primitive idealization (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Imposing more positive qualities on an external object or person than they actually have while ignoring their negative features<br><br>* Common in individuals with <u>personality disorders</u><br><br><br> | <br>* A woman believes that her new boyfriend is absolutely flawless.<br><br> |
| Blocking (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Temporarily or transiently inhibited thinking when feeling increased levels of <u>stress</u><br><br>* Commonly manifests when the affected individual is experiencing embarrassment<br><br><br> | <br>* An individual is unable to answer a question during an exam but immediately recalls it once the exam is over.<br><br> |
| <u>Hypochondriasis</u> (<u>psychiatry</u>) | <br><br>* Exaggerating or overemphasizing an illness to avoid responsibility or guilt associated with loneliness, <u>bereavement</u>, or aggressive impulses<br><br>* Common in individuals with <u>anxiety disorders</u> and/or a history of traumatic clinical experiences [[32]](/library/xtXEf-)<br><br><br> | <br>* A woman with mild abdominal cramps claims to be bedridden when nobody calls her on her birthday.<br><br> |
| Identification (psychiatry) | <br><br>* The unconscious modeling of one's behavior, characteristics, qualities, or traits, whether good or bad, on those of another person<br><br>* May be associated with <u>anxiety disorders</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* A young girl begins to dress more and more like her revered older cousin, without realizing it.<br><br>* A boy who was abused by his father becomes an abusive parent.<br><br><br> |
| Passive aggression (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Expressing aggression toward others indirectly in a nonconfrontational way<br><br>* Common in children and individuals with <u>BPD</u><br><br><br> | <br>* An employee appears to accept critique to their work but later reacts by procrastinating and avoiding work-related messages.<br><br> |
| Somatization (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Converting psychological problems into real bodily symptoms<br><br>* May be associated with <u>somatic symptom disorders</u><br><br><br> | <br>* A medical student develops <u>headaches</u> during a stressful board exam.<br><br> |
| Undoing (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Trying to avoid guilt about negative thoughts or actions by engaging in the opposite behavior<br><br>* Common in individuals with <u>OCD</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* After a man thinks about harming another person, he becomes overly accommodating to them.<br><br>* An individual with <u>OCD</u> has frequent and distressing thoughts about germ contamination and washes their hands until they're raw or bleeding.<br><br><br> |
| Fixation (psychiatry) | <br><br>* The cessation of development of <u>personality</u> at one of the childhood stages such as oral, anal, or phallic (compare with regression)<br><br>* May be associated with <u>anxiety disorders</u><br><br><br> | <br>* An individual fixated at the oral stage of development bites their <u>nails</u>, chews on a pen, or sucks their thumb in response to a stressful situation.<br><br> |
| Fantasy (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Withdrawal into fantasy to resolve inner and/or outer conflicts<br><br>* May be associated with stressful situations and personal crises<br><br><br> | <br>* An elderly man in a wheelchair repeatedly suggests to his grandson that they race one another on foot.<br><br> |





### Neurotic defenses [[33]](/library/KGbUZv)




| Overview of <u>neurotic defenses</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Description | Examples |
| Controlling (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Excessively attempting to manage or regulate the environment (i.e., objects or people) to minimize <u>anxiety</u><br><br>* May be associated with <u>OCD</u> or <u>anxiety disorders</u><br><br><br> | <br>* A mother does not let her child attend a friend's birthday party unless she can influence who else will attend it.<br><br> |
| Displacement (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Shifting an emotion to a less threatening or neutral object or person<br><br>* Distinct from projection<br><br>* Projection: The affected individual extends emotions/thoughts about themselves to another person.<br><br>* Displacement: The affected individual shifts emotions/thoughts about one person to a less threatening person or object.<br><br>* Common response to acute <u>anxiety</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* A man punches a wall after an argument with a colleague rather than confronting them.<br><br>* A mother demonstrates feelings of anger towards her child instead of her husband, who is the actual source of her frustration.<br><br><br> |
| Intellectualization (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Using abstract, rational, and/or logical reasoning to avoid affective expression and distance oneself from <u>stress</u><br><br>* Common response to emotional <u>stress</u><br><br><br> | <br>* A woman reacts to the diagnosis of a terminal illness with excessive investigation into the pathophysiology of and treatment modalities for the disease.<br><br> |
| Isolation of affect (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Separating or repressing an idea from the associated effect or idea<br><br>* Accepting reality without the accompanying emotional response<br><br>* Common response to emotional <u>stress</u> or a traumatic event<br><br><br> | <br>* A young man recalls traumatic events without showing any emotions.<br><br> |
| Rationalization (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Offering excuses or feasible explanations in an attempt to justify behaviors, attitudes, or beliefs to avoid self-blame<br><br>* Common in <u>OCD</u><br><br><br> | <br>* A student claims that she failed a grade because all her teachers dislike her, instead of admitting that she has not studied all year.<br><br> |
| Reaction formation (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Complete denial and/or rejection of an unacceptable impulse by acting in a diametrically opposite manner to avoid <u>anxiety</u>-provoking thoughts<br><br>* Associated with <u>anxiety disorders</u> (compare with <u>sublimation</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* A <u>homosexual</u> individual is highly critical of same-sex couples.<br><br> |
| Repression (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Thoughts are unconsciously removed from conscious awareness.<br><br>* Certain facts that were known and accepted at some point in life become absent from <u>memory</u> (compare with suppression).<br><br><br> | <br>* An adult suffers a <u>drowning</u> experience as a child and develops an intense fear of swimming later in life, with no <u>memory</u> of the childhood experience.<br><br> |
| Externalization (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Perceiving one's own <u>personality</u> in the external world and in external elements (including instinctual impulses, conflicts, moods, attitudes, and styles of thinking)<br><br>* Blaming others for the way one treats themself<br><br>* May be associated with <u>ADHD</u> or <u>substance use disorders</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* A man perceives his partner as aggressive and himself as peaceful, although he is the aggressor.<br><br>* A mother blames her son for preventing her from having friendships, although she chooses to spend all her time with her son.<br><br><br> |
| Dissociation (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Temporarily modifying personal identity, <u>memory</u>, consciousness, or motor activity in an extreme manner to avoid emotional <u>distress</u><br><br>* The affected individual usually has partial/no recollection of the traumatic incident.<br><br>* See “<u>Dissociative disorders</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br>* An individual who was abused as a child feels detached from their own body when they come into contact with their abuser.<br><br> |
| Sexualization (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Endowing an object, person, or function with sexual significance<br><br>* Sexualization of a person is usually linked to sexual objectification of that individual.<br><br><br> | <br>* A woman evaluates her partner based on their sexual significance only, excluding other characteristics.<br><br> |
| Inhibition (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Consciously limiting ego functions, alone or in combination, to avoid <u>anxiety</u> arising out of conflict<br><br>* May be associated with <u>anxiety disorders</u><br><br><br> | <br>* A parent is unable to discipline a disobedient child out of fear of making them angry.<br><br> |





### Mature defenses [[34]](/library/PDaWe5)




| Overview of mature defenses |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Description | Examples |
| Sublimation (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Shifting focus of unacceptable or unattainable impulses toward goal-directed activities<br><br>* Typically directing impulses in a more socially acceptable direction (compare with <u>reaction formation</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* An athlete uses their feeling of anger to motivate their training for a marathon.<br><br> |
| Altruism (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Serving others constructively to experience a personal vicarious experience and to cope with difficult stressors<br><br>* Resolving guilty feelings by meeting the needs of others (compare with <u>reaction formation</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* A rich woman gives a homeless man her lunch.<br><br> |
| Suppression (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Consciously postponing attention to an <u>anxiety</u>-provoking thought<br><br>* A temporary reaction that is easily recalled with the right stimulus (compare with repression)<br><br><br> | <br>* A resident suppresses her fear of blood during <u>surgery</u> to provide necessary patient care.<br><br> |
| Humor (psychiatry) | <br>* Using comedy to express feelings and thoughts to lessen personal discomfort and avoid emotional <u>distress</u> without producing an unpleasant effect on others<br><br> | <br>* A new employee expresses a serious situation in the form of a joke.<br><br> |
| Anticipation (psychiatry) | <br><br>* Realistic planning or premature worrying about future discomforts<br><br>* Associated with goal-directed behavior<br><br><br> | <br>* An A-student goes over course notes in preparation for a lecture the following morning.<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> “SASHA is a mature adult”: Sublimation, Altruism, Suppression, Humor, Anticipation are mature defenses.

## Coping strategies

* Definition: behavioral and mental strategies or skills that can be mobilized by an individual to aid in handling external and internal stressors (e.g., <u>stress</u>, illness) [[35]](/library/Xpc9LW0)[[36]](/library/cpcaoW0)

* Adaptive coping: behavioral and mental strategies that aid in responding to stressors in a positive and constructive manner [[35]](/library/Xpc9LW0)[[36]](/library/cpcaoW0)[[37]](/library/5Gci-d0)

* Examples

* Problem-focused coping: strategies that target the underlying cause of <u>stress</u> (e.g., ergonomical workplace to prevent and relieve health issues such as <u>back pain</u>)

* Emotion-focused coping: strategies that reduce the negative emotions associated with a <u>stressor</u> (e.g., responding to a misfortune with humor, distancing, or acceptance)

* Meaning-focused coping: cognitive strategies used to find meaning in or change the perspective on the stressful situation (e.g., <u>meditation</u>, <u>mindfulness</u>, positive reappraisal, reordering life priorities)

* Social coping: seeking support within a community to reduce <u>stress</u>

* Further categorized into

* Reactive coping: strategies pursued in response to a <u>stressor</u>

* Proactive coping: strategies pursued in anticipation of a <u>stressor</u>

* Maladaptive coping: conscious as well as unconscious thought patterns and behaviors engaged in for the short-term relief of <u>stress</u> that, however, increase <u>stress</u> in the long term. [[35]](/library/Xpc9LW0)[[36]](/library/cpcaoW0)

* Examples: rumination, anger, disengagement, <u>recreational drug</u> or <u>alcohol</u> use

* Persistence increases the risk of :

* <u>Major depressive disorder</u>

* <u>Anxiety disorder</u>

* <u>Sleep disorders</u>

* <u>Substance use disorders</u> and <u>drug-seeking behavior</u>

* Self-harm
